intro: Confucius and Mencius taught about how people should treat one another. They used key words like ren, li and yi. They described a kind of person they called the junzi. This unit explains those words and where they appear in the texts.

You will read short passages from the Analects and the Mencius. You will meet the five relationships and the famous story of Mencius's mother. You will see how Mencius argued that people are born with sprouts of goodness, and how another Confucian, Xunzi, disagreed.

By the end, you can explain each key word with a passage. You can tell what Mencius meant by the four sprouts. You can describe how readers, past and present, have agreed and disagreed about these teachings.
bigQuestion: What did Confucius and Mencius teach about being a good person and living well with others?

timeline.t: Confucius is born in Lu (traditional date)
Mencius is born in the state of Zou (traditional, approximate)
Mencius visits kings such as King Hui of Liang
Xunzi teaches that goodness must be learned
Liu Xiang gathers stories, including Mencius's mother
Zhu Xi makes the Mencius one of the Four Books
James Legge publishes the Analects and the Mencius in English
Reformers in China question old rankings and call for equal rights

write.prompt: Are people born good? Explain what Mencius argued, using Mencius 2A.6 (the child at the well) and 6A.8 (Ox Mountain) in Legge's translation. Then tell how Xunzi saw it differently, and how one passage from the Analects (such as 7.29) fits in.
tips: Name the book and passage number each time.
Say 'Mencius argued' or 'Xunzi taught'; do not state your own belief as fact.
Use unit words like ren, compassion and four sprouts.

title: Key Teachings of Confucius

chapters.title: Ren, Li and the Junzi
chapters.bigQuestion: What did Confucius think makes a person truly good?

story.title: The Bow She Forgot
story.kicker: A new student forgets to bow and wonders whether manners really matter.
paragraphs: It was Ana's first week at a Chinese weekend school in Chicago. She sat in the back row. When the teacher walked in, every student stood up and bowed a little. Ana stayed in her seat. Her cheeks went hot.
At break, a boy named Wei sat next to her. 'Don't worry,' he said. 'I forgot too, my first week.' Ana asked, 'Why do we even bow? Isn't it just a rule?'
Wei thought about it. 'My grandpa says it is like saying thank you with your body,' he said. 'He says Confucius taught about manners a lot. But he also said manners without a kind heart are empty.'
After break, the teacher came back in. Ana stood with the others and bowed. It felt strange at first. Then she noticed the teacher smile and bow back to the class.
That night Ana asked her mom, 'Can a bow be kind, or is it only polite?' Her mom said, 'That is a question people have asked for 2,500 years.' Ana decided to keep asking it.
story.think: Can good manners show real care? Can they ever be empty? Give an example.

lessons.title: What Ren Means
lessons.mainIdea: Ren, the central virtue in the Analects, means humaneness: caring for other people.
reading: The word *ren* appears over 100 times in the Analects. It is the most important virtue in the book. English translators use words like humaneness, goodness, kindness or benevolence. Legge often wrote 'perfect virtue.'
A student named Fan Chi once asked Confucius what ren means. Confucius gave a short answer. He said it means to love people. That answer is in Analects 12.22.
The Chinese character for ren is made of two parts. One part means person. The other part means two. Many readers say this shows that ren is about how people treat each other, not about being alone.

words.d: humaneness; caring for other people, the central virtue in the Analects
a good quality in a person, shown in how they act

look.title: Fan Chi's Question
look.text: Fan Chi asked about ren. The Master said: it is to love people.
look.cite: Analects, book 12, passage 22, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1861)
look.prompt: Why do you think Confucius gave such a short answer to a big question?

check.q: What does ren mean?
check.why: Ren means humaneness or caring for others. Ritual is li; doing right is yi.

check.q: How did Confucius answer Fan Chi in Analects 12.22?
choices: Ren is to obey the king
Ren is to follow the Dao
check.why: He said ren is to love people.

check.q: What two parts make up the character for ren?
check.why: The parts mean person and two, which many readers link to how people treat each other.

lessons.title: The One-Word Rule
lessons.mainIdea: Confucius taught: what you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
reading: In Analects 15.23, a student named Zigong asked for one word to guide a whole life. Confucius answered with the word *shu*. Legge translated it as reciprocity. Others say consideration or empathy.
Then Confucius explained. What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others. This is sometimes called the Silver Rule, because it is said in a 'do not' form.
Many traditions have a teaching like this. Readers often compare it to the Golden Rule in the Christian Gospels. Scholars discuss how the 'do not' and 'do' forms are alike and different.

words.d: reciprocity or consideration; thinking of others as you think of yourself
treating others the way you want to be treated

look.title: Analects 15.23
look.text: Zigong asked: Is there one word that can guide a person's whole life? The Master said: Isn't it reciprocity? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
look.cite: Analects, book 15, passage 23, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1861)
look.prompt: Think of a moment at school when this rule could help. What would you do?

check.q: Who asked for one word to guide a whole life?
check.why: Zigong asks this in Analects 15.23.

check.q: What word did Legge use to translate shu?
check.why: Legge translated shu as reciprocity.

check.q: Why is the teaching sometimes called the Silver Rule?
choices: It is said in a 'do not' form
check.why: It says what not to do, while the Golden Rule says what to do.

lessons.title: Ren Is Close at Hand
lessons.mainIdea: Confucius taught that ren is not far away: a person who truly wants it can start now.
reading: Some people thought goodness was only for great heroes. Confucius said something different. In Analects 7.29, he asked, is ren really far away? He said it more simply than they expected.
He answered his own question. If I truly want ren, he said, it is right here. Many readers take this as hope. Anyone can begin to act with care, today.
But Confucius also said ren is hard to keep up every day. He praised his student Yan Hui for keeping to it for months. So readers see two sides: ren is close, and it takes practice.

words.d: doing something again and again to get better at it
being kind, fair and caring toward others

look.title: Analects 7.29
look.text: The Master said: Is ren far away? If I want ren, here it is.
look.cite: Analects, book 7, passage 29, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1861)
look.prompt: What is one small way a person could show ren today?

check.q: What does Analects 7.29 say about ren?
choices: It is found only in old books
If you truly want it, it is close at hand
check.why: Confucius says ren is here if you truly want it.

check.q: Which student did Confucius praise for keeping to ren for months?
check.why: The Analects praises Yan Hui for this.

check.q: What two sides of ren do readers see?
choices: It is close, and it takes practice
check.why: Ren is near at hand, but keeping it takes daily practice.

lessons.title: What Li Means
lessons.mainIdea: Li means ritual and good manners: the set ways people show respect in daily life and ceremonies.
reading: The word *li* first meant rituals, like ceremonies to honor ancestors. Confucius used it more widely. Li also means everyday manners: how you greet, bow, sit, eat and speak.
In Analects 12.1, Confucius's favorite student Yan Hui asked about ren. Confucius told him to guide himself by li. Do not look, listen, speak or move in ways that go against li.
So in the Analects, li and ren go together. Li gives care a shape people can see. A bow, a greeting or a thank-you are small forms of li. Readers still discuss how the two fit.

words.d: ritual and good manners; the set ways people show respect
a ceremony or action done in a set way, often to show honor

look.title: Analects 12.1
look.text: Yan Hui asked how to practice ren. The Master said: Do not look at what is against li. Do not listen to what is against li. Do not speak or act in ways that are against li.
look.cite: Analects, book 12, passage 1, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1861)
look.prompt: What four things does Confucius say to guide by li?

check.q: What did li first mean?
check.why: Li first meant ritual. (The li that measures distance is a different Chinese word.)

check.q: In Analects 12.1, who asked Confucius about ren?
check.why: Yan Hui asks in 12.1, and Confucius points him to li.

check.q: How do li and ren go together in the Analects?
choices: Li gives care a shape people can see
check.why: Li is the visible form care takes.

lessons.title: Manners With a Heart
lessons.mainIdea: Confucius taught that ritual without a caring heart is empty.
reading: Confucius did not want empty manners. In Analects 3.3 he asked: if a person has no ren, what good is li to them? What good is music to them? Manners, for him, were meant to carry real feeling.
In Analects 3.4, someone asked about the root of li. Confucius said that in a funeral, deep sorrow matters more than perfect details. In ceremonies, it is better to be simple than showy.
Readers say this means li should come from the heart. A bow done with care means something. A bow done only to look good means much less, Confucius taught.

words.d: really meaning what you say or do
a formal event done in a set way, like a wedding or funeral

look.title: Analects 3.3
look.text: The Master said: If a person has no ren, what has he to do with li? If a person has no ren, what has he to do with music?
look.cite: Analects, book 3, passage 3, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1861)
look.prompt: In your own words, what is Confucius saying about manners without care?

check.q: What does Analects 3.3 say about li without ren?
check.why: Confucius asks what good li is to someone without ren.

check.q: What did Confucius say matters most at a funeral?
check.why: In 3.4 he says sorrow matters more than perfect details.

check.q: What does sincere mean?
check.why: Sincere means you truly mean it.

lessons.title: Li at School
lessons.mainIdea: Everyday school habits, like greeting and taking turns, are modern examples of what Confucius called li.
reading: Li is not only for ancient China. Every school has its own customs. Students line up, raise hands and greet visitors. Each custom helps people live and learn together.
Confucius taught that small customs matter. They help people know what to expect. They also show respect in a way others can see and understand. They make a shared life run more smoothly.
Customs differ from place to place. A bow in one school may be a handshake or a wave in another. Readers of the Analects often say the respect matters more than the exact form.

words.d: a usual way of doing something in a group or place
showing that you think someone matters

look.title: Customs in a Classroom
look.text: In Room 12, students greet the teacher with 'Good morning.' They raise hands to speak. They say 'thank you' when someone passes papers. At the end of the day, they push in their chairs for the custodian.
look.prompt: Which of these customs would Confucius call li? What care does each one show?

check.q: Which is a school example of li?
check.why: Taking turns to speak is a custom that shows respect.

check.q: Why do customs help, as Confucius taught?
choices: They help people know what to expect and show respect
check.why: Customs give respect a shared, visible form.

check.q: What do many readers say matters most in a custom?
check.why: Readers often say the respect matters more than the exact form.

lessons.title: Yi: Doing What Is Right
lessons.mainIdea: Yi means doing what is right, even when another choice would bring more gain.
reading: Another key word is *yi*. It means rightness or doing what is right. Legge translated it as righteousness. It asks: what is the fair and proper thing to do here?
In Analects 4.16, Confucius compared two kinds of people. The junzi, he said, understands what is right. The small person understands only what brings profit.
Confucius did not say gain is always bad. In Analects 4.5 he says people want wealth and honor. But he taught that they should not be gained in the wrong way.

words.d: rightness; doing what is fair and proper
gain, especially money, from something you do

look.title: Analects 4.16
look.text: The Master said: The junzi understands what is right. The small person understands what brings profit.
look.cite: Analects, book 4, passage 16, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1861)
look.prompt: Think of a choice where the right thing and the profitable thing are different. What would each person do?

check.q: What does yi mean?
check.why: Yi means rightness. Ren is humaneness; li is ritual.

check.q: In Analects 4.16, what does the small person understand?
check.why: Confucius says the small person understands profit.

check.q: Did Confucius say wealth is always bad?
choices: No, but it should not be gained the wrong way
check.why: Analects 4.5 says wealth should not be gained wrongly.

lessons.title: The Junzi
lessons.mainIdea: The junzi is the 'exemplary person' Confucius described: someone good because of how they act, not their birth.
reading: The word *junzi* once meant the son of a lord, a person of noble birth. Confucius changed how it was used. For him, a junzi is noble because of character, not family.
Translators write 'exemplary person,' 'gentleman' or, in Legge's words, 'the superior man.' The junzi learns, practices ren and li, and does what is right.
The Analects often contrasts the junzi with the 'small person.' In 14.29, Confucius says the junzi is modest in speech but goes beyond it in action. He does more than he says.

words.d: the exemplary person Confucius described, good by character rather than birth
being a good example for others
of high rank, or having fine character

look.title: Two Kinds of Person
look.text: Student A talks a lot about helping others but rarely does it. Student B says little, but quietly stacks chairs, helps a new student and keeps promises. Analects 14.29 says the junzi is modest in words and goes further in deeds.
look.prompt: Which student acts more like the junzi Confucius described? Explain with the passage.

check.q: What did junzi first mean?
check.why: Junzi first meant a person of noble birth.

check.q: How did Confucius change the idea of junzi?
choices: It meant noble by character, not birth
check.why: For Confucius, character made a junzi.

check.q: What does Analects 14.29 say about the junzi?
choices: He talks more than he acts
He is modest in words and goes further in deeds
check.why: The junzi does more than he says.

lessons.title: Learning and Thinking
lessons.mainIdea: Confucius taught that learning and thinking must go together, and both lead to practice.
reading: The Analects opens with learning. In 1.1 Confucius asks: isn't it a joy to learn and to practice what you learn? For him, learning meant changing how you live.
In Analects 2.15, he said learning without thinking is wasted. Thinking without learning is dangerous. A good student reads, asks questions and thinks it through.
Many Confucian readers say this is how a person becomes a junzi. You study good examples. You think about them. Then you practice, again and again, in real life.

words.d: to think carefully about something
in the Analects, studying and practicing so that you grow in character

look.title: Analects 2.15
look.text: The Master said: Learning without thinking is wasted work. Thinking without learning is risky.
look.cite: Analects, book 2, passage 15, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1861)
look.prompt: Give an example of learning without thinking, and one of thinking without learning.

check.q: What does Analects 2.15 say about learning without thinking?
check.why: Confucius says learning without thinking is wasted.

check.q: What does Analects 2.15 say about thinking without learning?
check.why: He says thinking without learning is risky or dangerous.

check.q: For Confucius, what should learning lead to?
check.why: Analects 1.1 links learning to practice in life.

review.q: Which word means humaneness, caring for others?
Which word means ritual and good manners?
Which word means doing what is right?
What does 'junzi' mean in the Analects?
choices: An exemplary person, good by character
review.why: Confucius used junzi for a person noble in character.

review.q: Which passage says, 'What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others'?

choices: Li without ren has little value
review.why: Confucius asks what good li is to someone without ren.

review.q: What does Analects 7.29 say about ren?
choices: It is close if you truly want it
review.why: Confucius says ren is here if you want it.

review.q: Who does Analects 4.16 say understands only profit?
review.why: The small person understands profit; the junzi understands what is right.

chapters.title: Five Relationships and Mencius's Sprouts
chapters.bigQuestion: Are people born with the seeds of goodness, and what helps those seeds grow?

story.title: Three Houses
story.kicker: A mother moves house three times until her son copies the right neighbors.
paragraphs: An old Chinese story tells of a boy named Meng Ke and his mother. The boy's father had died, and his mother raised him alone. At first they lived near a graveyard.

Little Meng Ke watched the funerals. Soon he was playing funeral in the yard, pretending to dig graves and weep. His mother frowned. 'This is not the place for my son to grow up,' she said. So they moved.
Next they lived beside a busy market. The boy watched the sellers. Soon he was playing market, shouting prices and bargaining with pretend coins. His mother shook her head. They moved again.

This time they lived next to a school. The boy watched the students bow to their teacher. He watched them read and practice ceremonies. Soon he was bowing and reciting too. His mother smiled. 'This is the place,' she said. They stayed.
The boy grew up to be Mencius, one of the most famous teachers in Chinese history. People still tell this story about his mother. Many use it to talk about how much our surroundings shape us.
story.think: Why did the mother keep moving? How do the places around you shape what you do?

lessons.title: Five Pairs
lessons.mainIdea: Confucian teaching names five key relationships, each with its own duties.
reading: Confucian thinkers wrote about five key *relationships*. They are ruler and subject, parent and child, husband and wife, older and younger sibling, and friend and friend.
The book Mencius lists them in 3A.4. It names a quality for each pair. Parent and child should share affection. Ruler and minister should share rightness. Friends should share trust.
The other two pairs have their own qualities in that list. Husband and wife each have their own roles. Older and younger should keep a proper order. Together, the five describe a whole society.

words.d: the way two people are connected, like parent and child or friends
ruler and subject, parent and child, husband and wife, older and younger sibling, friend and friend

look.title: Five Pairs
look.cite: Mencius 3A.4, as translated by James Legge, The Works of Mencius (1861)
look.prompt: Which of the five pairs is between equals?

check.q: Which is one of the five relationships?
check.why: Parent and child is one of the five.

check.q: Where does the book Mencius list the five relationships?
check.why: Mencius 3A.4 lists them. 2A.6 is the child at the well.

check.q: What quality does Mencius 3A.4 name for friends?
check.why: Friends should share trust or faithfulness.

lessons.title: Duties Both Ways
lessons.mainIdea: In Confucian teaching, each side of a relationship has duties, not only the lower one.
reading: People sometimes think the five relationships are only about obeying. But Confucian texts give duties to both sides. A parent must care for a child. A ruler must care for the people.
In Analects 12.11, a duke asked Confucius about good government. Confucius said: let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son.
Readers say this means each person should live up to their role. A ruler who is cruel is not being a true ruler. Mencius went further and said the people matter most in a state.

words.d: something a person should do because of their role
the part a person plays, like parent, friend or leader

look.title: Analects 12.11
look.text: Duke Jing of Qi asked about government. Confucius said: Let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, and the son a son.
look.cite: Analects, book 12, passage 11, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1861)
look.prompt: What would it mean for a father to 'be a father' in this passage?

check.q: In Confucian teaching, who has duties in a relationship?
check.why: Both sides have duties, such as a parent caring for a child.

check.q: Who asked Confucius about government in Analects 12.11?
check.why: Duke Jing of Qi asked, and Confucius spoke of roles.

check.q: What does 'let the ruler be a ruler' mean, as readers explain it?
choices: Each person should live up to their role
check.why: Readers say each person should fulfill the duties of their role.

lessons.title: Hard Questions
lessons.mainIdea: People have debated the five relationships, especially the place of women, and they respond in many ways.
reading: Four of the five relationships put one person above the other. Only friends are equals. In old China, this often meant wives had less power than husbands. Daughters had fewer chances to study than sons.
Many people have questioned this. In the 1900s, Chinese writers and reformers criticized these rankings. They called for equal rights and schooling for girls and women.

Today readers respond in different ways. Some say the rankings belong to the past. Some keep the idea of care and duty but drop the ranking. Some scholars point to women who studied the classics long ago.

words.d: a person who works to change and improve a society
the same in value or rights

look.title: Two Responses
look.text: Reader A: The five relationships ranked people, and women were placed lower. That part should be left behind. Reader B: The idea that each role has duties of care is still useful, if everyone is treated as equal.
look.prompt: What does each reader keep, and what does each question?

check.q: How many of the five relationships put one person above the other?
check.why: Ruler-subject, parent-child, husband-wife and older-younger were ranked. Only friends were equals.

check.q: Who criticized these rankings in the 1900s?
check.why: Reformers in the 1900s called for equal rights for women.

check.q: What do some modern readers keep from the five relationships?
choices: The idea of care and duty, without the ranking
check.why: Some keep care and duty but drop the ranking.

lessons.title: The Second Sage
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius was a later Confucian teacher, often called the Second Sage, whose teachings fill a book of seven parts.
reading: *Mencius* is the Latin form of Mengzi, meaning Master Meng. He lived about a century after Confucius. Traditional dates are about 372 to 289 BCE, but these are not certain.
Mencius traveled from state to state. He talked with kings and tried to persuade them to rule with kindness. He also taught students who wrote down his talks.
The book Mencius has seven books, each in two parts, like 2A and 2B. Later Confucians called him the Second Sage, after Confucius. His book became one of the Four Books.

words.d: a Confucian teacher who lived about a century after Confucius; also the name of his book
a very wise person honored by a tradition

look.title: Two Teachers, Two Times
look.cite: Traditional dates; scholars treat Mencius's dates as approximate
look.prompt: About how many years passed between Confucius's death and Mencius's birth?

check.q: What does Mengzi mean?
check.why: Mengzi means Master Meng; in English, Mencius.

check.q: What did later Confucians call Mencius?
check.why: He was honored as the Second Sage, after Confucius.

check.q: How is the book Mencius divided?
choices: Seven books, each in two parts
check.why: It has seven books, each split into A and B.

lessons.title: Mencius's Mother
lessons.mainIdea: A famous story says Mencius's mother moved three times to find a good place for her son to learn.
reading: The story of the three moves comes from an old book of stories about women, the Lienü zhuan. It was put together by Liu Xiang around the first century BCE, long after Mencius lived.

The same book tells a second story. Once young Mencius quit his studies early. His mother cut the cloth she was weaving. She said quitting learning was like ruining the cloth. He went back to study hard.
Historians cannot check these stories. But people in China have told them for over 2,000 years. They honor Mencius's mother as a model of a caring, wise parent.

words.d: the places and people around you
a person others look to as an example

look.title: Cutting the Cloth
look.text: Mencius came home early from his studies. His mother took a knife and cut the cloth on her loom. 'Quitting your learning,' she said, 'is like my cutting this cloth.' After that, Mencius studied day and night.
look.cite: Liu Xiang, Biographies of Exemplary Women (Lienü zhuan), book 1, story of the mother of Mencius, retold simply
look.prompt: Why do you think the mother chose to cut her cloth to teach this lesson?

check.q: Why did Mencius's mother move three times?
choices: To find a good place for him to learn
check.why: She wanted him near good examples, finally a school.

check.q: Where does the story of the moves come from?
check.why: It is told in Liu Xiang's Biographies of Exemplary Women.

check.q: What did the mother cut to teach a lesson?
check.why: She cut her weaving to show what quitting does.

lessons.title: Talking With Kings
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius told kings to rule with humaneness and rightness rather than chasing profit.
reading: The book Mencius opens with a meeting. King Hui of Liang asks Mencius how he can profit the kingdom. It is found in Mencius 1A.1. It is one of the best-known scenes in the book.
Mencius answers: why must Your Majesty speak of profit? He says there is only humaneness and rightness. If everyone chases profit, from the king down, the kingdom will be in danger.
Mencius taught that a good ruler cares for the people like a parent. He said that if a ruler is cruel, the people may rightly turn away. This idea was bold in his time.

words.d: to try to get someone to agree or act by giving reasons
caring for other people; the English word for ren

look.title: Mencius 1A.1

lessons.title: The Child at the Well
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius argued that anyone who sees a child about to fall into a well feels alarm and care at once.
reading: Mencius told a famous example in Mencius 2A.6. Imagine you suddenly see a small child about to fall into a well. What would you feel? He asked his listeners to picture it clearly.
Mencius said anyone would feel alarm and *compassion*. You would not feel it to win praise, or to please the child's parents. You would simply feel it, right away.
Mencius used this example to argue that people are born with a feeling of care for others. He said a person without it would hardly be human. This is his way of showing that human nature is good.

words.d: feeling for someone who is suffering and wanting to help
what people are like from birth

look.title: Mencius 2A.6

lessons.title: Four Sprouts
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius taught that four feelings in every person are sprouts that can grow into four virtues.
reading: In the same passage, Mencius named four *sprouts*. A sprout is a tiny new plant. He said every person is born with four feelings that are like sprouts.
The feeling of compassion is the sprout of ren. The feeling of shame at doing wrong is the sprout of yi. Modesty is the sprout of li. Knowing right from wrong is the sprout of wisdom.
Sprouts are small. Mencius taught they must be cared for to grow into full virtues. Like plants, they need the right conditions, just as his mother looked for the right home.

words.d: a tiny new plant; for Mencius, a small inborn feeling that can grow into a virtue
compassion, shame, modesty and knowing right from wrong, which Mencius said grow into four virtues
good judgment about what is true and right

lessons.title: Ox Mountain and a Different View
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius said goodness can be damaged like a stripped mountain, while another Confucian, Xunzi, said goodness must be learned.
reading: In Mencius 6A.8, Mencius described Ox Mountain. Its trees were once beautiful. But people cut them down, and cattle ate every new shoot. Now it looks bare.
Mencius said people might think the mountain never had trees. But it did. In the same way, he said, a person who acts badly still had sprouts of goodness. They were just harmed.
Not all Confucians agreed. A later thinker, *Xunzi*, taught that human nature tends toward selfishness. He said goodness comes from learning and ritual. Readers still compare the two views.

words.d: a later Confucian thinker who taught that goodness must be learned through study and ritual
a bare hill in Mencius's story, used to show how goodness can be damaged

look.title: Two Confucian Views
look.text: Mencius: People are born with sprouts of goodness. With care, they grow. When harmed, they wither, like Ox Mountain. Xunzi: People are born tending toward selfishness. Teachers, study and ritual shape them into good people, as a craftsman straightens wood.
look.prompt: How are these two views alike? How are they different?
